final_answer:
a hash table handles collisions when two keys hash to the same index. there are two main methods for resolving collisions: chaining and open addressing.

chaining uses a linked list (or another data structure like a binary search tree) at each bucket to store multiple entries that hash to the same index. this allows multiple entries to coexist at the same index without overwriting each other. the trade-off is that in the worst case, lookups can take o(n) time if many entries hash to the same index, though with a good hash function and resizing, it remains efficient. chaining is simple to implement and allows for dynamic resizing, but it uses extra memory for pointers.

open addressing stores all entries directly in the hash table array. when a collision occurs, it probes for an empty slot using techniques like linear probing (checking consecutive indices), quadratic probing (using a quadratic function), or double hashing (using a second hash function). the trade-off is that performance degrades as the table fills up, and deletions are more complex because removing an entry might leave gaps that affect probing. open addressing is more cache-friendly due to contiguous memory, but it requires careful handling of resizing and probing.

chaining is preferred when memory is not a constraint and lookup speed is crucial. open addressing is better when memory is tight and cache efficiency matters, but it requires more complex management of probing and resizing.
